items.abstract: <jats:p>Human infrastructure can affect wildlife by altering habitat access, human encounter risk, hunting pressure, and the spatial distribution of resources, but species may respond through different behavioral pathways. Some species may avoid infrastructure locally, others may shift the timing of activity, and many may show weak or context-dependent responses. We used camera-trap data from 483 stations across the Las Piedras region of Madre de Dios, Peru, to evaluate how distance from human infrastructure was associated with temporal activity and local use across 30 Neotropical mammal taxa. We modeled two complementary binomial responses: nocturnality, defined as the probability that independent detections occurred at night rather than during the day, and detection-night probability, defined as the probability that a species was detected on a given active camera night. Hierarchical generalized additive models estimated nonlinear species-specific and trophic-group responses to infrastructure distance while accounting for species identity, trail placement, spatial structure, survey grid, camera station, and relevant environmental covariates. The best-supported final models combined species-specific and trophic-group distance smooths, while trophic-group-only models remained strongly unsupported. Across the primary near–far contrast from 0.85 to 7.20 km from infrastructure, responses were uneven across both species and response dimensions. Lowland tapir showed the clearest temporal response, with predicted nocturnality higher near infrastructure than farther away. Detection-night responses were generally smaller in absolute magnitude, but small rodents showed higher predicted detection-night probability nearer infrastructure and collared peccary showed higher predicted detection-night probability farther from infrastructure. Brocket deer showed a similar positive but less certain detection-night trend farther from infrastructure, and tayra showed a small, supported increase in detection-night probability nearer infrastructure. Many carnivores showed weak, nonlinear, or uncertain near–far detection-night responses. Overall, Amazonian mammals did not respond to human infrastructure through a single behavioral pathway. Instead, temporal and local-use responses were concentrated in particular taxa and ecological contexts, highlighting the value of evaluating when species are active alongside where they are detected.</jats:p>
title: The night shift: temporal activity and local use respond unevenly to human infrastructure in an Amazonian mammal community

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The grey wolf (
                      <jats:italic>Canis lupus</jats:italic>
                      ) is an important apex predator whose persistence in human-dominated landscapes is increasingly influenced by livestock depredation and negative human perceptions. This study investigated grey wolf diet composition, reported livestock depredation patterns, and community perceptions in Orakzai District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Field surveys were conducted from August 2024 to July 2025 across 25 purposively selected sites. Grey wolf scats were collected and analysed using morphological characteristics and microscopic examination of prey remains. Structured household interviews were conducted with 123 respondents across 25 villages. Firth penalized logistic regression was used to assess factors associated with negative rather than neutral perceptions of grey wolves.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 29 wolf scats yielded 30 identified prey occurrences representing 15 prey species. Wild prey accounted for 17 occurrences (56.67%), whereas domestic prey accounted for 13 (43.33%). Wild boar (
                      <jats:italic>Sus scrofa</jats:italic>
                      ) was the most frequently detected prey species, followed by Asiatic palm civet (Paradoxurus hermaphroditus), while cattle (
                      <jats:italic>Bos taurus</jats:italic>
                      ) were the most frequently detected domestic prey. Dietary diversity was H′ = 2.52, with prey species richness of 15 and evenness of 0.93. These findings represent prey occurrences detected in scats and cannot establish prey preference or selection because prey availability was not independently quantified. All 123 respondents reported at least one livestock attack attributed to grey wolves. Most reported attacks occurred at night (61.0%), followed by evening (35.0%), and October had the highest frequency of reported attacks (20.5%). Overall, 80.5% of respondents expressed negative perceptions of grey wolves. The reported number of grey wolves killed during the previous 5–10 years was positively associated with the odds of negative rather than neutral perception (OR = 2.495, 95% CI = 1.453–4.740, P &lt; 0.001). Age, occupation, livestock holdings, wolf sightings, attack timing, and livestock injury were not statistically significant.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings highlight substantial interactions between grey wolves and livestock-dependent communities. They emphasize the need for evidence-based conflict mitigation, improved livestock protection, and conservation strategies informed by prey availability and local ecological conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Diet pattern and human grey wolf conflict in Orakzai District, Pakistan

items.abstract: <jats:p>Human-Elephant Conflict (HEC) has emerged as a critical conservation, governance and socio-environmental challenge in India; particularly in Odisha, where high elephant populations coexist with expanding human activities. Increasing human-elephant interactions have resulted in rising human fatalities, elephant deaths, crop loss, habitat fragmentation, and livelihood insecurity. This study examines the ecological, socio-economic, legal, and governance dimensions of HEC in Odisha with particular emphasis on compensation mechanisms, coexistence strategies, and conservation governance. The policy and practice review research paper adopts a qualitative and doctrinal research methodology based primarily on secondary data, including government reports, policy documents, wildlife literature, census records, and conservation studies. Through interdisciplinary analysis, the paper identifies habitat fragmentation, land-use change, mining activities, infrastructure expansion, climate variability, and socio-economic vulnerabilities as major drivers intensifying HEC in the state. The study further evaluates the effectiveness and implementation challenges associated with compensation mechanisms, and existing mitigation frameworks. The findings indicate that although Odisha possesses a comparatively structured compensation framework and several conservation initiatives, persistent governance challenges such as delayed compensation disbursement, fragmented institutional coordination, weak habitat governance, and inadequate community participation continue to undermine long-term conflict mitigation efforts. Comparative analysis of selected elephant-range regions and countries highlights the growing importance of coexistence-oriented governance approaches integrating habitat connectivity, scientific monitoring, community participation, land-use planning, and localized mitigation strategies. The paper argues that sustainable mitigation of HEC in Odisha requires a shift from reactive compensation-based responses toward integrated coexistence-oriented conservation governance. Strengthening habitat protection, improving compensation administration, enhancing institutional coordination, incorporating ecological considerations within developmental planning, and promoting community-based conservation strategies remain essential for reducing conflict intensity and fostering long-term human-elephant coexistence in Odisha.</jats:p>
title: Navigating human-elephant conflict in Odisha, India: unraveling the causes, impacts, and compensation paradigm

items.abstract: <jats:p>Scholars have proposed the adoption of a contemporary global taboo against bats to prevent the outbreak of diseases to which humans are susceptible (zoonotic diseases). Zoonotic disease outbreaks are driven by environmental change and can result in collective human traumas that span generations. The proposal inspired us to explore the extent and characteristics of traditional wildlife taboos for zoonotic disease risk mitigation. We conducted a literature review to assess the role of zoonotic disease as a catalyst for traditional taboo development and enculturation. Out of concern that contemporary taboos could facilitate or amplify collective human trauma, we also contemplated the ethics of constructing and promoting contemporary wildlife taboos to serve health security aims. In this Perspective, we report on our review of traditional wildlife taboos as they relate to zoonotic disease risk mitigation, noting information shortfalls and observable linkages. We also respond to the call for contemporary wildlife taboos by exploring neocolonial approaches to conservation and achieving public health goals; the dynamics of values, ethics, and morals; and potential adverse impacts on biodiversity conservation. We conclude that the historical role of taboos as risk mitigation measures is not well-established due to data limitations; linkages cannot be readily drawn between specific wildlife species and specific pathogens. However, in general, there appears to be a reasonable likelihood that some taboos arose when communities repeatedly observed human health problems following contact with certain wildlife species. We do not recommend contemporary taboos as risk mitigation measures. If “taboo campaigns” are developed, we urge socio-cultural sensitivity, knowledge, and community participation. To safeguard the affected communities, socio-cultural and ecological impact assessments should be conducted as standard practice.</jats:p>
title: Wildlife taboos as zoonoses risk mitigation: examining the past and proposed with considerations for human health and biodiversity conservation

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Climate change is increasingly affecting pastoral communities in sub-Saharan Africa through more frequent and severe droughts and floods, threatening livelihoods, food security, and mental well-being. Pastoral women and children are particularly vulnerable because of their dependence on livestock for nutrition, income, and cultural identity. This study assessed the psychosocial and livelihood impacts of climate change among pastoral women in Kenya and evaluated community-based interventions to strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A mixed-method baseline survey was conducted among 1,138 women in Kajiado, Narok, and Taita Taveta counties following severe drought in 2022 - 2024. Data were collected using structured questionnaires, focus group discussions, and Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) measurements for 941 children below 10 years. In partnership with the county government, 401 women from 18 women's groups and 342 learners from five schools were trained in climate-smart mushroom and vegetable production. The impact of the interventions was evaluated among 194 women and 204 learners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Most baseline survey respondents (64%) were aged below 35 years, 74.3% depended on casual labor, and 13% had no source of income. Narok recorded the highest proportion of children (33%) with poor nutritional status. During the drought, 347 mothers reported being unable to feed their children, while 86% received no food assistance. The most reported impacts were mental health problems (58%), resource conflicts (45%), and starvation (40%). More than half (58%) expressed a need for mental health intervention and support. The introduced farming practices were new to most participants. Among the women trained, 87% rated mushrooms as highly acceptable and 45% incorporated them into household diets. Among learners, 83% participated in training and 39% practiced mushroom cultivation at school.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The interventions improved dietary diversity, promoted alternative livelihoods, and strengthened community resilience. Participants also reported increased hope, social cohesion, and confidence. These findings demonstrate that expanding livelihood options and demonstrating alternative ways to grow food and improve nutrition can reduce the collective trauma of communities already burdened by poverty, demographic pressure, early marriage, and pregnancy, while strengthening their resilience the next time prolonged drought strikes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Climate change trauma and social-ecological resilience building: insights from pastoral women in Kenya

<jats:p>
                    The common ostrich (
                    <jats:italic>Struthio camelus</jats:italic>
                    ), despite its global classification as Least Concern, has experienced severe population declines in Zimbabwe, particularly within Lake Chivero Recreational Park (LCRP). This study assessed community perceptions, legal knowledge, and traditional uses of ostriches among 79 households in Maine, Mwashita, and Caroline villages, using a stratified random sampling design covering 28% of the household frame. Weighted estimates indicated that 59.0% of households could identify ostriches and 69.2% considered them important for conservation, yet only 55.7% reported willingness to notify authorities of sightings, revealing a perception–behaviour gap. Correct legal knowledge of wildlife law was critically low (16.9%), with village-level disparities highlighting localized enforcement gaps. Ethnobiological analysis showed moderate diversity of ostrich-related uses (UV = 1.39) and strong consensus on medicinal applications (IAR = 0.905), dominated by bone use (UAV = 68.2%). These findings demonstrate that ostrich conservation in LCRP is constrained by limited legal literacy, persistent traditional practices, socio-economic pressures, and the disconnect between positive attitudes and conservation action. Effective interventions must therefore move beyond awareness-building to strengthen procedural knowledge, institutional trust, and culturally sensitive alternatives, while extending benefit-sharing mechanisms to remote communities. Integrated strategies of this nature are essential to secure the long-term persistence of ostrich populations in Zimbabwe.
                  </jats:p>
title: Local perceptions on ostrich conservation in farming areas around Lake Chivero Recreational Park, Zimbabwe

items.abstract: <jats:p>Counter-poaching patrols are a primary tool for protecting wildlife in threatened landscapes, yet detection rates of active poaching incursions are typically low and patrol planning frameworks that have been operationalised and performance-assessed remain rare. We describe a structured search framework applied over a decade of counter-poaching operations in the Kenyir Core Area, Malaysia, 1,200 km² of mountainous tropical forest critical to Malayan tiger recovery. Drawing on search theory and actor-based crime scripting, we developed a network of prioritised patrol routes based on poacher terrain use, termed Operational Patrol Space (OPS). This was combined with a vigilance metric that tracks time elapsed since each route was last patrolled. This two-stage framework guides rangers first to detect initial sign of an active incursion using OPS patrol routes, then to fix the precise location of the active poaching team using targeted search lines within a reduced search region. Following implementation, active incursion detection rates increased from 16% to 50% and success pinpointing the active camp location rose from 20% to 56%, with patrol team numbers held constant. We discuss transferability to other protected area contexts and provide sufficient methodological detail for the framework to be replicated and adapted by other teams.</jats:p>
title: Catching needles in haystacks: a structured search framework to optimise counter-poaching patrols

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Understanding the psychological determinants of pro-environmental behavior is critical in addressing the escalating climate crisis. Despite increasing recognition of an important predictor of environmentally responsible actions, the role and interaction of eco-emotions remain insufficiently examined. This gap is particularly evident in non-Western contexts such as India.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine the influence of environmental identity on pro-environmental behavior, with particular attention to the role of eco-emotions within this relationship. The study further examines the mediating roles of eco-anxiety and eco-hope, and the moderating effect of eco- hope on the identity–anxiety–behavior pathway. A cross-sectional survey design was employed, collecting data from 395 adults across India (ages 18–60, Indian residents, fluent in English, no diagnosed mental illnesses) via convenience sampling using online questionnaires. Measures included the Environmental Identity Scale by Clayton, Hogg Eco-Anxiety Scale by Hogg, Climate Change Hope Scale by Li and Monroe, and Pro-Environmental Behaviour Scale by Markle. Regression, mediation, and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using SPSS PROCESS.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results indicated that environmental identity significantly predicted pro-environmental behavior, with eco-anxiety partially mediating this association. Eco-hope did not independently mediate pro- environmental behavior and did not moderate the indirect effect of identity through eco-anxiety.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that interventions promoting environmental identity should simultaneously cultivate constructive concern and realistic hope, optimizing engagement in sustainable behaviors. The study contributes to the understanding of identity–emotion–behavior dynamics in environmental psychology and underscores culturally contextualized strategies to foster climate action.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Eco-anxiety and eco-hope shaping the relationship between environmental identity and pro-environmental behavior: from self to action

<jats:p>
                    Southern Africa holds an irreplaceable stock of locally adapted livestock breeds that persist mainly within smallholder and communal production systems. These breeds are losing genetic ground because of uncontrolled crossbreeding, disrupted land tenure, climate driven destocking, and decades of livestock policy that rewarded commercial output over the conservation of indigenous breeds. This structured narrative review, which incorporates systematic elements in its search and screening but does not follow the full protocol of a systematic or scoping review, examines how indigenous knowledge systems (IKSs) may function as a conservation mechanism for animal genetic resources (AnGR) across the region, drawing on 62 peer-reviewed and grey-literature sources published between 1995 and 2026 and retained in the final thematic synthesis. Findings synthesized across six thematic domains suggest that IKS-associated practices are linked to several dimensions of
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    conservation, although the underlying evidence is predominantly cross-sectional, observational, and ethnographic, and does not permit strong causal inference. Phenotype-based selection criteria appear, in the studies reviewed, to be associated with the persistence of some adaptive traits, though the genetic mechanisms underlying these associations are largely unconfirmed. Communal institutions such as livestock loaning (mafisa) and rotational bull-sharing are reported, mainly on ethnographic grounds, to regulate gene flow and limit inbreeding in the absence of any pedigree recording system. Customary taboos, socio-cultural governance structures, and oversight by elder councils are documented as helping to anchor indigenous genotypes within community gene pools across generations. Molecular studies of populations managed under IKS report heterozygosity, allelic richness, and between-breed differentiation that are consistent with, though not proof of effective community-level genetic management; the available evidence indicates an association between IKS-informed management and conservation-relevant genetic patterns rather than a demonstrated causal relationship. Significant gaps remain, particularly the limited genomic validation of IKS selection claims, the systematic under-documentation of women’s knowledge in small-stock management, and the near-total absence of longitudinal research linking IKS practice to genetic outcomes over time; closing these gaps is identified as the priority for establishing whether the associations described here reflect genuine conservation mechanisms. The review closes with policy-relevant recommendations for further evaluating, and where warranted embedding, IKS within national AnGR strategies and SADC livestock frameworks.
                  </jats:p>
title: The role of indigenous knowledge systems in conserving animal genetic resource biodiversity in Southern Africa: a review

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) contains highly diverse aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems but remains underrepresented in biodiversity research. Environmental DNA (eDNA) offers a non-invasive approach for biodiversity assessment, yet its application across SSA has not been comprehensively synthesized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic review following PRISMA 2020 was conducted using Google Scholar and Scopus for studies published from January 2018 to April 2026. Eligible peer-reviewed English-language studies used eDNA or DNA metabarcoding to assess aquatic or terrestrial biodiversity in SSA. Data were extracted on geographic distribution, ecosystems, target taxa, markers, sequencing platforms, sampling approaches, reference databases, and reported constraints.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. Aquatic ecosystems accounted for 88% of studies, while fish were the dominant target taxon (48%). Southern Africa had the largest geographic representation. The most frequently used marker was 12S rRNA (52%), and Illumina was the dominant sequencing platform (72%). Incomplete reference databases were reported as a major limitation in 68% of studies, while terrestrial and arthropod-focused applications were markedly underrepresented.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>eDNA has demonstrated substantial potential for biodiversity monitoring in SSA, particularly in aquatic systems. However, incomplete reference libraries, methodological heterogeneity, logistical constraints, contamination risks, limited infrastructure, and capacity gaps constrain broader application. Future work should strengthen African reference databases, standardize methods, expand terrestrial and arthropod applications, and support SSA-led capacity development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Environmental DNA (eDNA) applications for biodiversity monitoring across countries in the Sub-Saharan African region: a systematic review

<jats:p>
                    The Nile crocodile (
                    <jats:italic>Crocodylus niloticus</jats:italic>
                    ) is classified as of Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. As apex predators, crocodiles play vital ecosystem clean-up roles. However, anthropogenic activities threaten its population in wetlands in Southern Africa. The species attracts significant interest from humans within the Traditional Water Knowledge (TWK) domain. This Preferred Reporting Items of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-guided review assessed the uses of crocodiles, inclusion levels, and barriers and benefits of integrating TWK in Southern African Development Community (SADC) countries’ wildlife and water policies for crocodile conservation. TWK poses an existential threat to crocodile conservation through intergenerational negative perceptions bordering on myths and ethnozoological medicinal use incorporating its eyes, tail, head, scales, gall bladder, belly skins, liver, and bile duct secretions. Anthropogenic-driven destruction of nesting sites abetted by poor monitoring of wetland habitats by wildlife authorities causes declines in populations and shifts in distribution. Crocodile ranching is effective to sustain populations of crocodiles though its reliance on wild egg collection for enhancing production negates its overall contribution to conservation. TWK is poorly conceptualized and covered in wildlife and water conservation policies in SADC. Integrating geospatial techniques and citizen science in TWK provides a holistic framework to conserve crocodile populations in Southern Africa.
                  </jats:p>
title: Traditional water knowledge and Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus) conservation in Southern Africa: a systematic review of policy integration, institutional gaps, cultural uses, and barriers
